opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the really exciting frontiers. Today's models can attend to on the order of a million or a few million tokens in context, which is already remarkable. You can put in a long document, a few hours of video, or a decent-sized codebase. But what you'd really like is the illusion that the model can attend to trillions of tokens: all of the internet, or all of your personal information if you've opted in, like your email, your documents, and your photos. You'd want it to bring any piece of that to bear when it's answering your question.

I don't think you get there by naively scaling up the attention mechanism. Standard attention is quadratic, and even with a lot of clever tricks, a trillion tokens of full attention just isn't computationally feasible. So the way I think about it is more like a multi-stage system. You have very cheap, lightweight mechanisms that narrow trillions of tokens down to maybe millions of plausibly relevant pieces. Then you use progressively more sophisticated and expensive models to whittle that down to the tens of thousands or hundred thousand tokens that really matter. Finally, your most capable model reasons deeply over that smaller set. That's similar in spirit to how search systems have worked for a long time: lots of candidates, a cascade of increasingly careful ranking, and then the really careful work on the final set.

The difference now is that each of those stages can be much more semantic. You're not just matching words. You're understanding what the person is actually trying to do and which pieces of information are relevant to that intent. The really interesting research questions are about making that whole pipeline learned end to end, so the retrieval and attention aren't separate bolted-on components but part of one system.

There's also a hardware and systems angle that I find fascinating. How do you lay out that much state across memory hierarchies so you can access the right parts quickly? I think algorithmic improvements and hardware co-design together will get us much closer to that experience of a model that effectively has access to everything relevant, rather than just whatever fits in the context window.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most exciting directions, honestly. Right now we have models with context windows of a million, maybe a few million tokens, and that's already pretty useful. You can put a whole codebase in there, or a bunch of long documents, and the model can reason over it. But a million tokens is really not that much when you think about what you'd actually want.

What I'd love is for a model to be able to attend to trillions of tokens. So think about something like, all of the code at Google, or all of the papers in a field, or everything you've personally read or written over your life, or the entire web. And not in a retrieval-augmented way where you pull out the top ten snippets and hope you got the right ones, but really having the model able to attend to all of it with the kind of fidelity it currently gets on in-context information. Because in-context information is treated very differently from what's baked into the weights. It's much more precise, much more faithful.

Now, the naive approach obviously doesn't work. Attention is quadratic, and even linear scaling to a trillion tokens is enormous. So I don't think you get there with brute force. I think you need a bunch of algorithmic ideas. Things like hierarchical attention, where you have coarse summaries and you can drill down. Things like caching and sharing. If a lot of users are attending to the same large corpus, you shouldn't recompute that every time. You should precompute some representation of that corpus once and have many requests share it. There's a lot of systems engineering in there as well as ML research.

The other thing I'd say is there's a nice distinction between the kind of knowledge that should be in the weights and the kind that should be in context. Weights are great for general knowledge about the world and about how to reason. Context is great for very specific, often private or fast-changing information. And if you can make context very, very large, then you can keep the weights fairly general and still personalize or specialize the model enormously just by what you put in front of it. You don't need to fine-tune a model for every company or every person.

So I'm fairly optimistic. I don't think it's going to be one big breakthrough, I think it'll be a series of improvements, each giving you maybe 10x, and a few of those stacked together gets you a long way. And I think the result is going to be qualitatively different in terms of what these systems can do.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is how you give a model access to that much information without requiring it to do an enormous amount of computation for every token it generates. You probably don’t want to attend equally to every part of a trillion tokens. You want the system to identify which pieces are relevant, look at those more closely, and perhaps go back for additional information as it reasons through a problem.

There’s a useful analogy to how we work. You have access to a huge amount of information, but when someone asks you a question, you don’t read everything you’ve ever read before answering. You bring a few relevant things to mind, and sometimes you look something up. I think there’s a lot of room to make that process more integrated into the model, so that finding information and using it are learned together.

And then the measure of success isn’t just, can you put a trillion tokens somewhere the model can access? It’s, can it reliably find the important details and combine information from different places? That’s what would make that scale of context really useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how much computation you need to apply to each token. If you have trillions of tokens available, you probably don’t want to process all of them equally for every question. You want the system to identify which pieces are relevant, look at those more carefully, and perhaps go back for more information as it reasons.

That starts to blur the distinction between a context window and a retrieval system. What you really want is the ability to use an enormous amount of information, with the cost of answering a question tied more closely to the information needed for that answer than to the total amount you have stored. Doing that efficiently, while still finding an important connection between two very distant pieces of information, is a really interesting challenge.
